intervals.label: construction and installation
intervals.locator: INSPIRE experiment record 1110643, fields date_approved and date_completed
intervals.note: Start = date_approved (1998-09-17). VERIFIER NOTE (2026-09-17): end = INSPIRE's date_completed field, re-fetched and confirmed to read '2008-09' verbatim (not fabricated). But this field is NOT a routine construction-milestone field: on ATLAS's INSPIRE record (1108541) and on LHCf's (1126263), the same date_completed field reads '9999', which both those records correctly treat as INSPIRE's placeholder for 'ongoing, not completed' rather than a real date (see experiment:lhcf's interval note). LHCb is likewise an active, non-terminal experiment, so a literal 'completed' date is intrinsically implausible; unlike ATLAS/LHCf, LHCb's record has an actual date in this field rather than the placeholder, which is most likely either (a) a genuine INSPIRE data-entry anomaly, or (b) a real but differently-scoped milestone (e.g. detector installation/construction complete, consistent with first collisions 14 months later) that INSPIRE's schema does not distinguish from experiment completion. No source independent of this one INSPIRE field corroborates a September 2008 construction-complete date for LHCb, so confidence is downgraded from 'verified' to 'uncertain' and this interval must not be read as asserting LHCb 'completed' in 2008 (it is deliberately given the non-terminal status 'construction', not 'completed', for exactly this reason). Re-verify against the LHCb JINST detector paper or an LHCb-specific installation announcement if either becomes fetchable.

intervals.label: Long Shutdown 2 / LHCb Upgrade I installation
intervals.note: CONFLICT/nuance: the LHC-wide Long Shutdown 2 ended and Run 3 pp collisions began on 5 July 2022 (see accelerator:lhc), but LHCb's own outreach page dates the completion of Upgrade I *installation* specifically to April 2023, nine months later. This record follows the LHCb-specific completion date rather than the LHC-wide Run 3 start, since Upgrade I (new VELO, new tracker, removal of the hardware trigger) is an LHCb-specific programme; the discrepancy likely reflects LHCb running in a partial/commissioning capacity for the first months of Run 3 while Upgrade I installation finished. No source fetched in this session resolves this explicitly.

physics_goals.quote: The Large Hadron Collider beauty (LHCb) experiment specializes in investigating the slight differences between matter and antimatter by studying a type of particle called the "beauty quark", or "b quark".
physics_goals.value: Study CP violation and rare decays of b (beauty) and c (charm) hadrons to probe the matter-antimatter asymmetry of the universe

summary.plain: LHCb is one of the four big experiments at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Instead of surrounding the collision point on all sides, its detector is shaped like a single forward cone, built to catch particles containing beauty and charm quarks and study why the universe has so much more matter than antimatter.
summary.technical: Single-arm forward-spectrometer experiment at LHC Point 8 (Ferney-Voltaire, France), covering low pseudorapidity in the forward direction to exploit the strongly forward-peaked production of b-hadrons and c-hadrons at hadron colliders. Proposed by Letter of Intent in August 1995, approved September 1998, installed by September 2008, first collisions November 2009. Physics programme centres on CP violation and rare decays of heavy-flavour hadrons; Upgrade I (new VELO, silicon tracker, removal of the hardware trigger) was installed by April 2023.

unique_capabilities.quote: Instead of surrounding the entire collision point with an enclosed detector as do ATLAS and CMS, the LHCb experiment uses a series of subdetectors to detect mainly forward particles - those thrown forwards by the collision in one direction.
unique_capabilities.value: A single forward-arm spectrometer (not a 4-pi enclosure) optimised for the forward-peaked production of b and c hadrons at a hadron collider
